summary: Separate a single random walker from the distribution over states, and compare convergence or oscillation under a declared transition matrix and initial distribution.
objective: Build a small Markov chain in space where I can step the distribution vector and compare it with a sampled walker.
intent_signals: Show how a Markov chain settles into a stationary distribution.
Compare one random walker with the distribution over all states.
example_prompts: Build a Markov chain state graph with a distribution bar per state and a stepping control.
Show the two-state swap chain alternating from a nonuniform start and staying fixed from its uniform stationary distribution.
negative_signals: Not a hidden Markov model, inference or learning recipe.
Not a claim that every chain converges: periodic and reducible chains must be shown as exceptions.
not_for: Not a hidden Markov model, inference or learning recipe.
Not a claim that every chain converges: periodic and reducible chains must be shown as exceptions.

entities.name: State nodes
entities.guidance: Place states as distinct 3D nodes with room above each for a probability bar, since the distribution is the real subject.

entities.name: Transition arcs
entities.guidance: Draw directed arcs with visible probability labels; arcs with probability zero should be absent rather than drawn faintly.

entities.name: Walker and distribution
entities.guidance: Show one sampled walker and the numerically propagated distribution side by side, with the propagation tolerance stated, so a sample path is distinct from a distribution.

state_contract.model: A finite state set with a row-stochastic transition matrix of finite nonnegative entries whose rows sum to one, a row-vector distribution updated as p_next = p P in floating point with a stated tolerance, a seeded walker sampled from the current row, and a stationary vector solved from the balance equations. An all-zero row is rejected rather than renormalised, and periodicity is reported from the chain structure independently of what the current run displays.
state_contract.authority: The transition matrix is authoritative. The distribution uses deterministic floating-point propagation with the stated tolerance, while the walker is a sample; the two are never blended into one display.
actions: Step or run the sampled walker.
Edit a transition probability and renormalise the row.
Reset the distribution to a chosen initial state.

invariants: Every row stays finite, nonnegative and sums to one after any edit; an all-zero row is refused rather than renormalised, and negative or non-finite entries are rejected before any propagation.
The distribution vector always sums to one; drift indicates numerical error and must be reported.

Report periodicity from the chain structure independently of observed convergence. For the two-state swap matrix [[0,1],[1,0]], a nonuniform starting distribution alternates and the uniform distribution stays fixed. Do not generalise oscillation to every nonstationary start of every periodic chain; some such starts can reach or converge to a stationary distribution.
motion_guidance: Animate probability mass flowing along arcs proportional to its contribution, so a step is legible as redistribution.
Do not fade the walker between nodes as if it were partially in two states; the jump is discrete.
known_limits: Finite discrete-time chains only; continuous-time and infinite state spaces are out of scope.

Propagation is deterministic floating-point matrix arithmetic with a stated tolerance rather than exact rational arithmetic, so reaching a fixed vector on screen is a numerical observation, not a proof about the chain.
Authored guidance only: no scene runtime, rendering or numerical calibration has been run for this recipe.
A periodic irreducible finite chain still has a unique stationary distribution; what it lacks is the start-independent limiting behaviour quoted in the aperiodic theorem.

claims.statement: A stationary distribution satisfies pi equals pi times the transition matrix, and a limiting distribution is the limit of the n-step state probabilities independent of the starting state.
For a finite irreducible aperiodic chain the equations pi equals pi P together with the normalisation have a unique solution, and that solution is the limiting distribution.
claims.scope: Conditions matter: reducible or periodic chains fall outside this statement.

source_refs.locator: 11.2.6, uniqueness theorem for irreducible aperiodic chains

object_craft.structure: Solid node bodies with a flat top platform for the probability bar and a base ring for the sampled visit count.
object_craft.material: Neutral node material with one accent reserved for the walker, so a node never looks selected merely because it is probable.
object_craft.articulation: Nodes are static; only bars and the walker move.

object_craft.structure: Curved tubes with arrowheads offset from the node surface and a label plate at the arc midpoint.
object_craft.material: Arc thickness encodes probability with a legend, and the label carries the exact value so thickness is never the only cue.
object_craft.articulation: Arc geometry rebuilds when probabilities change.

physical_contract.scope: Deterministic matrix propagation in floating point with a stated tolerance, plus sampled jumps for the walker; no continuous dynamics.
checks: The distribution sums to one at every step within tolerance.
For the two-state swap matrix, verify alternation from a declared nonuniform start and a fixed distribution from the uniform start, while reporting period 2 in both cases.
